summary: A revision of RFC 2301 describing the TIFF representation of image data used for Internet fax. It is based on feedback and on independent implementation and interoperability testing since 1998, with changes summarized in an annex.

plainLanguage.summary: A fax machine sends a compressed image, not a page of text. This document says how to put that image into a TIFF file, using only the fields that every TIFF reader understands and filling them with the values the fax standards use, so that a program can tell a plain fax from a colour one. It also defines six profiles, from a minimal black-and-white set that every implementation must handle to one that puts several codings on the same page.

subtitle: How a fax image is stored in a TIFF file so that a fax over the Internet and a fax over the telephone network look the same.

tldr.problem: A fax is a compressed image, and the format used to carry it over the telephone network is defined by the ITU. Sending a fax by email means the image has to be wrapped in something that can travel in a mail message, and the wrapping has to be faithful enough that a gateway can print it on a real fax machine.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines TIFF-FX, a profile of TIFF that uses a subset of the Baseline TIFF fields with values that match the ITU-T Group 3 recommendations, and adds new fields where colour fax needs them. It defines six profiles, from the minimal black-and-white one to mixed raster content.
tldr.outcome: Every implementation must support Profile S, the minimal black-and-white set, and every colour implementation must support Profile C. The file format is carried in mail messages with the image/tiff and image/tiff-fx content types, and the document obsoletes RFC 2301.

facts.label: Fax profiles
facts.value: S, F, J, C, L and M

today: RFC 3949 is a Draft Standard published in February 2005 and has not been obsoleted. It obsoleted RFC 2301, which described the same file format, and it defines the six profiles from the minimal black-and-white one that every implementation must support to the mixed raster content one. Its files travel in mail messages with the image/tiff and image/tiff-fx content types.

sections.title: Introduction: The Six Fax Profiles
sections.content:
This document describes the use of TIFF, the Tag Image File Format, to represent the data content and structure generated by the current suite of ITU-T Recommendations for Group 3 facsimile. It supports six profiles. Profile S is the minimal black-and-white profile, using binary MH compression. Profile F is the extended black-and-white profile, using binary MH, MR and MMR compression. Profile J is the lossless JBIG black-and-white profile. Profile C is the lossy colour and grey-scale profile, using JPEG compression. Profile L is the lossless colour and grey-scale profile, using JBIG compression. Profile M is the mixed raster content profile, which uses a combination of existing compression methods. Each profile corresponds to the content of an ITU-T Recommendation and is a subset of the full TIFF for facsimile specification.

Profile S describes a minimal interchange set of fields that guarantees at least binary black-and-white images will be supported, and every implementation is required to support it. With the intent of specifying a file format for Internet fax, the document specifies the structure of TIFF files for facsimile data, defines ITU fax-compatible values for existing TIFF fields, and defines new TIFF fields and values required for compatibility with ITU colour fax. The resulting specification is known as TIFF-FX, and references to the format should always use that name, because some profiles in it may not be interpreted correctly by other TIFF applications.

The profiles form a tree. Profile S, the minimal profile, is based on Modified Huffman compression. Profile F specifies Modified Huffman, Modified READ and Modified Modified READ compression. Every implementation of TIFF for facsimile must implement Profile S, which is the root of the tree, and every colour implementation must implement Profile C. An implementation of a particular profile must also implement the profiles on the path that connect it to the root, and may optionally implement profiles off that path: an implementation of Profile M must also implement Profiles C and S and may optionally implement F, J or L, while an implementation of Profile C must also implement Profile S and may optionally implement F or J.

The document recommends a TIFF file structure compatible with low-memory and page-level streaming implementations, and notes that unless otherwise stated the current TIFF specification and selected technical notes are the primary references for describing TIFF, while this document is the primary reference for the field values used by fax applications.
sections.plainLanguage: There are six profiles, and they are layered. The minimal one, a plain black-and-white fax, is the base that everything else must include, and the colour one is the base that everything else with colour must include. The layering means a program that claims to handle the most capable profile can also handle the simpler ones, because the simpler ones are part of it.

sections.title: The TIFF File Structure
sections.content:
TIFF provides a means for describing, storing and interchanging raster image data, which makes it a good match for facsimile documents, since those are multi-page raster images. Each raster image consists of a number of rows or scanlines, each with the same number of pixels, the unit of sampling. Each pixel has at least one sample or component, exactly one for black-and-white images.

A TIFF file begins with an 8-byte image file header. The first two bytes describe the byte order used within the file: the legal values are II, 0x4949, when bytes are ordered from least to most significant, and MM, 0x4D4D, when they are ordered the other way within a 16- or 32-bit integer. Either byte order can be used, except in the minimal black-and-white profile, which must use II. The next two bytes contain the value 42, which identifies the file as a TIFF file, and the last four bytes give the offset to the first image file directory. An IFD can be at any location in the file after the header, but must begin on a word boundary.

An IFD is a sequence of tagged fields, sorted in ascending order by tag value. It consists of a 2-byte count of the number of fields, a sequence of field entries, and a 4-byte offset to the next IFD. Each field entry has 12 bytes: a 2-byte tag, 2 bytes identifying the field type, 4 bytes giving the count of values or offsets, and 4 bytes holding either the offset to a value stored outside the IFD or the value itself. Each separate raster image in the file is represented by an IFD.

A TIFF file can hold more than one IFD, organised either as a linked list, with the last entry pointing to zero, or as a tree, using the SubIFDs field in the primary IFD. Child IFDs describe related images, such as a reduced resolution version of the primary image. All fax profiles represent a multi-page fax image as a linked list of IFDs, with a NewSubfileType field containing a bit that identifies the IFD as one page of a multi-page document, and each IFD has a PageNumber field giving the page number in ascending order.
sections.plainLanguage: The file starts with eight bytes: two saying which way round the numbers are, two carrying the value 42 that marks the file as TIFF, and four giving the offset of the first directory. A directory is a sorted list of tagged fields describing an image and pointing at its data, and each field entry is 12 bytes. A multi-page fax is a list of these directories, one per page, linked to each other.

sections.title: The TIFF Fields Used by Fax
sections.content:
The TIFF specification defines a commonly used core set of fields known as Baseline TIFF, and the technical notes define several extensions. The TIFF-based specification for fax uses a subset of the Baseline fields with selected extensions, and in a few cases defines new TIFF fields specifically for fax applications. The document lists the fields required for all fax profiles, the additional fields required for all fax profiles, the fields recommended for all fax profiles, and the new fields recommended for fax profiles.

The fields used only by particular profiles are described in the sections on those profiles, together with the ITU-compatible field values, that is, the image parameters, for each profile. The full set of permitted fields is the one in the TIFF specification, and the profile sections define subsets of it, each section ending with a table summarising the required and recommended fields for that profile and the values they can have. Annex A gives a summary of the TIFF fields used or defined in the document as a convenient reference for implementors.

A general rule runs through the document: specifying the file structure alone is not normally enough to describe the capabilities of a recipient, and sufficient detail should be provided to exclude any unsupported features. For extended Internet fax, the image file structure and the image coding should always be specified.
sections.plainLanguage: Most of the document is a list of TIFF fields and the values a fax should give them. Some fields apply to every fax, and each profile adds its own. Each profile ends with a summary table, and the annex collects all the fields in one place for implementors.

sections.title: Profile S: The Minimal Black-and-White Profile
sections.content:
Profile S is the minimal black-and-white subset of TIFF for facsimile, and all implementations must support it. Black-and-white mode is the binary fax application most users are familiar with, and it is appropriate for black-and-white text and line art. The minimal interchange portion supports one-dimensional Modified Huffman compression with the original Group 3 fax resolutions, commonly called standard and fine. There are no recommended fields in this profile, the file must be little-endian, that is, the byte order value in the header must be II, and a single strip must contain the image data for each page.

The summary table gives the field values that make up the minimal interchange set. The baseline fields are: BitsPerSample, 1; Compression, 3 for one-dimensional Modified Huffman coding, with T4Options set to 0 or 4; FillOrder, 2, least significant bit first; ImageWidth, 1728; ImageLength, the total number of scanlines in the image; NewSubfileType, 2, where bit 1 identifies a single page of a multi-page document; PageNumber, the page number followed by the total page count; PhotometricInterpretation, 0, where a pixel value of 1 means black; ResolutionUnit, 2, meaning inch; RowsPerStrip, the number of scanlines per strip, which equals the ImageLength because there is one strip; SamplesPerPixel, 1; StripByteCounts, the number of bytes in the TIFF strip; StripOffsets, the offset from the beginning of the file to the single TIFF strip; XResolution, 204 or 200 pixels per inch; and YResolution, 98, 196, 100 or 200 pixels per inch.

The one extension field is T4Options, where 0 means MH coding with end-of-line codes that are not byte aligned, and 4 means MH coding with byte-aligned end-of-line codes. The document notes that where a field is a sequence of flag bits, an implementation should test the relevant bits individually so that later extensions to the sequence can be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: The minimal profile is a plain black-and-white fax: one bit per pixel, one-dimensional Huffman coding, and a page 1728 pixels wide. The file must be little-endian and each page must be in a single strip, which keeps a program that has very little memory able to process it. The resolutions allowed are the classic standard and fine ones, with 204 or 200 pixels across the page.

sections.title: Profile F: The Extended Black-and-White Profile
sections.content:
Profile F is the extended black-and-white profile, and it provides the standard definition of TIFF-F. It extends the minimal interchange set of fields with a richer set of black-and-white capabilities, adding the required baseline, extension and new fields, and the recommended ones. The document devotes a section to the technical implementation issues that this profile raises.

Those issues are the ones that a program writing or reading a file has to get right. They cover how the image data is divided into strips, the order in which the bits within a byte are stored, how multiple pages are laid out, and the compression used. There is also an example of how the page-quality fields are used, practical guidelines for writing and reading multi-page TIFF-F files, and a description of using TIFF-F for streaming applications.

The document then lists implementation warnings, each of which is a mistake that a codec or file writer can make and that breaks the file for a fax reader: uncompressed data, encoding and resolution, end-of-line codes that are not byte aligned, end-of-line codes themselves, the exclusion of the return-to-control sequence, and the use of the end-of-facsimile-block for compressed images. Each warning says what to do instead, so that a file produced by one program is read correctly by another.
sections.plainLanguage: The extended black-and-white profile is the richer version of the minimal one, and it is the format people usually mean when they say TIFF-F. Most of the section is a list of the mistakes that break a fax file: the wrong bit order, end-of-line codes that are not byte aligned, uncompressed data, and the wrong handling of the return-to-control marker.

sections.title: Profile C and Profile L: Colour
sections.content:
Profile C is the base colour profile, required in all colour implementations, and covers the lossy JPEG representation of colour and grey-scale facsimile data. Profile L is the lossless colour and grey-scale facsimile profile, using JBIG compression. Both are defined in the same way as the black-and-white profiles: an overview, the required baseline, extension and new fields, the recommended fields, and a summary table of the required and recommended fields with their permitted values.

Profile C is the root of the colour tree, so anything that handles colour fax has to handle it. Profile L sits above it, and the mixed raster content profile above that.
sections.plainLanguage: Colour comes in two flavours: a lossy one using JPEG, which every colour implementation must support, and a lossless one using JBIG, which reproduces the image exactly. The lossless profile builds on the lossy one, so an implementation of the lossless one also handles the lossy one.

sections.title: Profile M: Mixed Raster Content
sections.content:
Unlike the previous fax profiles, which use a single coding method and resolution for an entire page, Mixed Raster Content enables different coding methods and resolutions within a single page. The example the document gives is a page holding black-and-white text, which is best coded with MMR or JBIG, a colour bar chart, best coded with JBIG, and a scanned colour image, best coded with JPEG. Similarly, although a spatial resolution of 400 pixels per inch may be best for the black-and-white text, 200 pixels per inch is usually enough for a colour image.

MRC does not define any new coding methods or resolutions. Instead it defines a three-layer image model for structuring and combining the scanned image data, applied here with the TIFF format to give a data structure that differs from the recommendation but applies the same coding methods, uses the same compressed image data streams, and is consistent with the TIFF principle of a single IFD per image.

The three layers are the Foreground and the Background, which are both multi-level, and the Mask, which is bi-level. Each layer may appear only once on a page and is coded independently of the other two. The final image is obtained by using the Mask layer to decide whether an output pixel comes from the Foreground or the Background layer: when the mask pixel value is 1 the corresponding pixel from the Foreground layer is selected, and when it is 0 the pixel from the Background layer is selected. Each layer is an image and, when present, is represented by at least one IFD in the file.
sections.plainLanguage: This profile lets one page hold several kinds of picture, each with its own coding and resolution, which is what a modern fax page needs: sharp text next to a colour photograph. The trick is the mask, a black-and-white layer that says, for every pixel, whether to take the colour from the foreground layer or from the background layer.

sections.title: MIME Types and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The MIME content types image/tiff and image/tiff-fx are used for TIFF-FX encoded image data, and the registrations of these content types are described elsewhere.

On security, the document describes a file format for Internet fax, which is a series of profiles of TIFF for facsimile. It does not create any security issues that have not already been identified for TIFF, and the new fields it defines are of a purely descriptive nature, so no new security risks are incurred. The encoding specified does not in any way preclude the use of any Internet security protocol to encrypt, authenticate or non-repudiate TIFF-encoded facsimile messages.
sections.plainLanguage: The file is sent with the ordinary image/tiff and image/tiff-fx content types. The format itself adds no security questions beyond the ones TIFF already has, because the extra fields only describe the picture. Nothing stops a sender from encrypting or signing the message with the usual Internet mail security protocols.
